root.text:
Fernhill Outdoor Annual Report 2026

Fernhill Outdoor Co. is a fictional company that designs and sells clothing, footwear and camping equipment for hiking and outdoor sports. This report covers the financial year from 1 January to 31 December 2026. All amounts are in US dollars unless stated otherwise, and comparisons are with the 2025 financial year.

children.title: Letter from the Chief Executive
children.summary: Maya Lindqvist reports Fernhill’s strongest year yet: revenue exceeded $490 million, operating income rose nearly a third, equipment led growth, and recycled materials reached 58% of fabric purchases. She notes challenges from trail-running shoe discounting and warm European weather, while highlighting $64.8 million in cash and no borrowings. The letter also outlines plans to open six stores and build a Netherlands distribution centre, and thanks employees and customers.
children.text:
2026 was our strongest year yet. Revenue passed 490 million dollars for the first time, growing 10.6 percent, and operating income rose by almost a third as more customers bought directly from us. Equipment was the standout: our new lightweight tent range sold out twice in the summer, and the segment grew faster than any other. We also kept our promise to use more recycled materials, which now make up 58 percent of the fabric we buy.

Not everything went to plan. Trail-running shoes faced heavy discounting across the market, and we cut our range rather than chase sales at a loss. A warm November in Europe slowed jacket sales for several weeks. Both reminded us why we keep a strong balance sheet: we ended the year with 64.8 million dollars in cash and no borrowings.

Next year we will open six new stores and start building a second distribution centre, in the Netherlands, so that orders reach European customers in two days instead of four. Thank you to our 2,140 colleagues and to every customer who chose Fernhill. Maya Lindqvist, Chief Executive.

children.title: 2026 at a Glance
children.summary: A table compares key 2026 measures with 2025, showing improvement across every measure: revenue rose 10.6%, gross margin increased 1.7 points, and operating income and net income grew about 30%. It also reports free cash flow, store count, and employee count; the text notes revenue growth across all segments and regions, stronger margins from direct-to-consumer sales, and free cash flow covering investment and the proposed dividend.
children.text:
The table below sums up the year. Every measure improved on 2025. Revenue grew in all three segments and all three regions, the gross margin widened as more sales came through our own website, app and stores, and free cash flow covered both the year's investment and the proposed dividend. Definitions of each measure are given in the Financial Review.

children.title: Strategy
children.summary: The section outlines the company’s 2025–2028 strategy and progress on its three priorities: growing direct sales, leading in lightweight camping equipment, and making products that last through repair and resale. It covers 2028 targets and review mechanisms, customer research informing the plan, and progress across sales channels, equipment launches and revenue, guarantees, repairs, and resale programmes. No tables or images are mentioned.

children.title: Our plan for 2025 to 2028
children.summary: Describes the company’s three priorities for its four-year plan: grow direct sales, lead in lightweight camping equipment, and make products that last longer and can be repaired or resold. It lists 2028 targets—direct sales above two thirds of revenue, $150 million in equipment revenue, and 75% recycled or responsibly sourced fabric—and notes that progress is reviewed twice yearly, partly tied to executive pay, and currently ahead of plan on direct sales and recycled materials. The plan was informed by a survey of 12,000 customers seeking lighter, longer-lasting gear.
children.text: In 2025 we set out a four-year plan with three priorities: sell more directly to customers, lead the market in lightweight camping equipment, and make products that last longer and can be repaired or resold. Behind each priority sit measurable targets for 2028: direct sales above two thirds of revenue, equipment revenue of 150 million dollars, and 75 percent recycled or responsibly sourced fabric. The board reviews progress against these targets twice a year, and part of executive pay depends on them, as described under Governance. Two years in, we are ahead of plan on direct sales and recycled materials and on track for equipment. The plan was shaped by a survey of 12,000 customers, who told us they wanted lighter gear that lasts longer.

children.title: Progress on our priorities
children.summary: This section brings together progress on three priorities: growing direct-to-customer sales, leading in lightweight equipment, and making products that last. It covers sales channels, app users and stores; the Aspen tent launch, equipment revenue and future models; and Fernhill’s extended guarantee, repairs, resale programme and plans to expand repair counters. No tables or images are mentioned.

children.title: Selling directly to customers
children.summary: Direct sales through the website, app and stores grew to 64% of revenue, supported by 1.3 million active app users who purchase more often than website-only customers. The company ended the year with 64 stores and continues to use wholesale to reach new customers, while focusing on fewer, larger retailers. Direct customer feedback informs product design, and the app supports boot-fitting bookings, nearby stock checks and five-year guarantee registration.
children.text: Direct sales, through our website, app and own stores, rose to 64 percent of revenue from 60 percent. The relaunched app now has 1.3 million active users, and app customers buy 2.4 times a year on average, against 1.6 times for website-only customers. We opened seven stores and closed one, ending the year with 64. Wholesale remains important to reach new customers, especially in countries where we have no stores, but we now sell to fewer, larger retailers. Customers who buy directly also tell us more: product reviews and repair requests now feed straight into our design teams. The app also lets customers book a boot fitting, check stock in a nearby store and register products for the five-year guarantee.

children.title: Leading in lightweight equipment
children.summary: The Aspen ultralight tent launch sold 41,000 units, making it the company’s most successful launch; the two-person model weighs 1.1 kilograms and won top lightweight-tent recognition from three outdoor magazines. Equipment revenue reached $113 million, on track for the 2028 target, supported by a doubled design team and a new Colorado test centre. A one-person version and a four-season model are planned for 2027.
children.text: The Aspen ultralight tent range, launched in April, was the most successful launch in our history, selling 41,000 units. Its two-person tent weighs 1.1 kilograms, lighter than any competitor at the same price. We doubled the equipment design team to 36 people and opened a test centre in Colorado where every tent spends a week in wind and rain machines before it goes on sale. Equipment revenue reached 113.0 million dollars, on track for the 2028 target. A one-person version and a four-season version will join the range in 2027. Independent reviewers named the Aspen 2 the best lightweight tent of the year in three outdoor magazines.

children.title: Making products that last
children.summary: Fernhill extended its product guarantee from two to five years, repaired 23,500 items, and resold 11,200 through its Second Life buyback programme in 2026. Repair and resale earned $2.9 million and customers using these services were twice as likely to buy again within a year; repairs are free during the guarantee and charged at cost afterward, most often for broken zips or torn seams. In 2027, Fernhill plans to add repair counters to the ten stores that do not yet have one.
children.text: We want customers to keep Fernhill products for longer. Every product now carries a five-year guarantee, up from two years, and our repair service fixed 23,500 items. The Fernhill Second Life programme buys back used products for store credit and resells them, and sold 11,200 items in 2026. Repair and resale together earned 2.9 million dollars, a small amount, but customers who use them are twice as likely to buy from us again within a year. In 2027 we will add repair counters to the ten stores that do not yet have one. Repairs are free within the guarantee and charged at cost after it, and the most common repairs are broken zips and torn seams.

children.title: Financial Review
children.summary: Reviews Fernhill’s 2026 financial performance across segment, channel, and regional revenue, including growth drivers and plans for 2027. It covers improved gross and operating margins, the factors affecting profitability, and the outlook for costs. It also summarizes cash flow, liquidity, inventory, the proposed dividend, and planned investments in distribution, stores, and an equipment test centre.

children.title: Revenue by segment
children.summary: Fernhill’s 2026 segment revenue totaled $493.5 million, up 10.6% from 2025. Apparel was the largest segment at $237.0 million and led every quarter, peaking in Q4; Equipment grew fastest at 15.0%, supported by the new tent range, while Footwear grew 7.2% amid competition and discounting. The table compares 2026 and 2025 revenue and growth by segment, and the chart shows quarterly 2026 revenue by segment.
children.text:
Fernhill reports three segments. Apparel is the largest and peaks in the fourth quarter with winter jackets. Equipment grew fastest, by 15.0 percent, from 98.3 to 113.0 million dollars, driven by the new tent range in the second and third quarters. Footwear grew more slowly as trail-running shoes faced strong competition and heavy discounting across the market.

| Segment | 2026 (millions) | 2025 (millions) | Growth |

| Apparel | 237.0 | 214.0 | +10.7% |
| Footwear | 143.5 | 133.9 | +7.2% |
| Equipment | 113.0 | 98.3 | +15.0% |

children.title: Revenue by channel
children.summary: Online sales through the company website and app rose to 41% of revenue, while own-store sales stayed at 23% and wholesale fell to 36%; the shift toward higher-margin direct sales lifted profitability. Online orders are fulfilled from the Ohio distribution centre, returns fell to 8.1% after fit guides were added, mobile accounted for 71% of online orders, and average spend per order increased to $128 from $119.
children.text: Online sales through our own website and app made up 41 percent of revenue, up from 37 percent. Our own stores made up 23 percent, the same as last year, and wholesale to independent outdoor retailers and department stores 36 percent, down from 40 percent. Direct sales carry a higher margin, because we keep the retailer's share, so the shift towards them lifted profitability. Online orders are fulfilled from our distribution centre in Ohio, and returns fell to 8.1 percent of online sales after we added fit guides to every product page. Mobile phones now account for 71 percent of online orders. Online customers also spent more per order, 128 dollars on average, up from 119 dollars.

children.title: Revenue by region
children.summary: The table reports 2026 revenue by region and growth versus 2025: North America remained largest at $256.6 million, while Asia-Pacific grew fastest at 23.2% and Europe grew 10.6%. Asia-Pacific growth followed new stores in Japan and an Australian retail partnership; Europe’s growth was tempered by warm weather delaying jacket sales. Euro- and pound-denominated revenue was 38% of the total, and the company plans to open its first South Korean store and expand wholesale in Australia and New Zealand in 2027.
children.text:
North America is still our largest market, but Asia-Pacific grew fastest, by 23.2 percent, after we opened our first two stores in Japan and started selling through a large Australian outdoor retailer. Europe grew 10.6 percent, held back by the warm November, which delayed jacket sales into December and January. Revenue earned in euros and pounds was 38 percent of the total, the source of our currency risk described under Risks. In 2027 we will open our first store in South Korea and expand wholesale in Australia and New Zealand.

| Region | 2026 (millions) | 2025 (millions) | Growth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| North America | 256.6 | 236.5 | +8.5% |
| Europe | 187.5 | 169.6 | +10.6% |
| Asia-Pacific | 49.4 | 40.1 | +23.2% |
| Total | 493.5 | 446.2 | +10.6% |

children.title: Profitability
children.summary: The section summarizes improved profitability, with gross margin rising to 47.8% and operating margin to 11.8%. It covers the drivers of higher gross profit—including more direct sales, lower freight costs, fewer sales events, and heavier shoe discounts—and operating-expense growth from new stores, launch marketing, and a larger design team. It also notes that freight costs are expected to remain roughly flat and operating expenses to grow more slowly than revenue in 2027, and estimates that each gross-margin point is worth about $4.9 million at this year’s revenue.

children.title: Gross margin
children.summary: Gross margin rose to 47.8% from 46.1%, driven by the shift to direct sales and normalized ocean freight rates, partly offset by heavier trail-running shoe discounts. Gross profit increased to $235.9 million from $205.7 million, while full-price sales grew to 78% of total sales as the company held fewer sales events. The section also notes that freight costs are expected to stay roughly flat in 2027 and estimates each gross-margin point is worth about $4.9 million at this year’s revenue.
children.text: Gross margin rose to 47.8 percent from 46.1 percent. About 1.2 points came from the shift to direct sales and about 0.8 points from lower ocean freight rates, which returned to normal levels after two expensive years. Heavier discounting of trail-running shoes took away about 0.3 points. Gross profit, revenue minus the cost of the products we sold, was 235.9 million dollars, up from 205.7 million. We expect freight costs to stay roughly flat in 2027. Each additional point of gross margin is worth about 4.9 million dollars of gross profit at this year's revenue, which is why we watch freight rates and discounting closely. Full-price sales made up 78 percent of the total, up from 74 percent, as we ran fewer sales events.

children.title: Operating expenses
children.summary: Operating expenses rose 10.4% to $177.6 million in 2026, growing more slowly than revenue as operating margin increased to 11.8% from 10.1%. The table breaks expenses down by type, with stores and selling the largest category; growth was driven mainly by new stores and Aspen tent launch marketing, while warehouse sorting machines helped slow distribution costs. Head office costs rose 11.8%, largely due to a larger design team, and are expected to grow more slowly than revenue in 2027.
children.text:
Operating expenses grew 10.4 percent to 177.6 million dollars, slightly slower than revenue, so operating margin reached 11.8 percent, up from 10.1 percent. Most of the increase came from new stores and from marketing for the Aspen tent launch. Distribution costs grew more slowly than sales thanks to new sorting machines in the Ohio warehouse. The table shows operating expenses by type. Head office costs grew 11.8 percent, mostly from a larger design team, and we expect them to grow more slowly than revenue in 2027.

| --- | --- | --- |
| Stores and selling | 82.4 | 75.0 |
| Marketing | 38.1 | 33.2 |
| Distribution | 31.6 | 29.8 |
| General and administrative | 25.5 | 22.8 |
| Total | 177.6 | 160.8 |

children.title: Cash flow and balance sheet
children.summary: Covers cash generation, liquidity, inventory management, and the company’s proposed dividend and investment priorities. It reports $37.2 million in free cash flow, $64.8 million in cash, no borrowings, and a $96.4 million year-end inventory balance; inventory turnover improved and stock fell despite higher sales. It also explains the proposed $0.42-per-share dividend and planned uses of cash, including distribution-centre, store, and equipment-test-centre investments.

children.title: Cash flow
children.summary: Operations generated $55.8 million, and capital spending of $18.6 million left free cash flow of $37.2 million, up 31.0%. The company paid a $14.4 million dividend, made no share buybacks, ended the year with $64.8 million in cash and no borrowings, and has an unused $80 million credit line available until 2029. It also reports cash held in short-notice accounts at three large banks and interest income of $2.1 million, up from $1.3 million.
children.text: Cash generated by operations was 55.8 million dollars. Capital spending was 18.6 million, mostly on new stores and warehouse automation, leaving free cash flow of 37.2 million, up 31.0 percent. We paid a dividend of 14.4 million for 2025 and bought no shares back. Cash at year end was 64.8 million dollars, up from 42.0 million, and we have no borrowings. An unused credit line of 80 million dollars is available until 2029 if we need it. Our cash is held with three large banks, in accounts that can be withdrawn at short notice. Interest earned on cash balances was 2.1 million dollars, up from 1.3 million.

children.title: Inventory
children.summary: Year-end inventory was $96.4 million, down 4% despite higher sales; inventory turnover rose from 2.4 to 2.7 times, helping cash flow improve more than profit. Weekly store-level planning and earlier transfers of slow-selling trail-running shoes to outlets reduced stock, and the company aims to keep inventory growth below sales growth in 2027. Older stock goes first to outlet stores and then to outdoor charities, with no products destroyed; lower year-end winter-jacket stock is expected to mean fewer January-sale discounts.
children.text: Inventory at year end was 96.4 million dollars, down 4 percent despite higher sales. We now plan stock for each store weekly instead of monthly and moved slow-selling trail-running shoes to our outlet stores earlier in the season. Inventory turned 2.7 times in the year, up from 2.4. Less money tied up in stock was the main reason cash flow improved more than profit did. We aim to keep inventory growth below sales growth in 2027 as well. Older stock is offered first to our outlet stores and then donated to outdoor charities; we do not destroy unsold products. Stock of winter jackets at year end was lower than last year, so we expect fewer discounts in the January sales.

children.title: Dividend and use of cash
children.summary: The board proposes a 2026 dividend of $0.42 per share, up from $0.36, costing about $16.8 million and payable in May 2027 if shareholders approve it at the annual meeting. The company targets dividends of about 40% of net income and plans to use remaining cash for a second distribution centre, new stores, and an equipment test centre; share buybacks are considered only if cash exceeds these needs. The dividend has increased every year since payments began in 2019.
children.text: The board proposes a dividend of 0.42 dollars per share for 2026, up from 0.36 dollars, which would cost about 16.8 million dollars and be paid in May 2027. Our policy is to pay out about 40 percent of net income as dividends. The rest of our cash will fund the second distribution centre, new stores and the equipment test centre. We will consider buying back shares only if cash stays above what those plans need. Shareholders will vote on the dividend at the annual meeting in May 2027. Since we started paying dividends in 2019, the dividend has grown every year.

children.title: Segment Performance
children.summary: This section summarizes performance across Apparel, Footwear, and Equipment, including revenue trends, key product drivers, and upcoming product plans. Apparel grew 10.7% to $237.0 million, led by jackets, while Footwear rose 7.2% to $143.5 million, entirely from hiking boots; trail-running shoes were flat. Equipment growth was led by tents, up 21% to $61 million, with packs, sleeping bags, and accessories up 9% to $52 million. The subsections can answer questions about product performance, customer feedback and returns, services, sourcing and suppliers, product improvements, and planned launches.

children.title: Apparel
children.summary: Apparel revenue rose 10.7% to $237.0 million, driven by jackets and strong fourth-quarter sales; recycled insulation, certified down, and high jacket margins also supported profitability. The section covers the new merino base-layer range’s first-year sales, everyday-wear growth, lower returns after website fit improvements, wool sourcing standards, and plans for women’s base-layer cuts in 2027.

children.title: Jackets and insulation
children.summary: Apparel revenue grew 10.7% to $237.0 million, with jackets accounting for just under half; the Ridgeline insulated jacket sold 182,000 units. All insulated jackets switched to recycled polyester fill and certified down at no added customer cost. A warm European November delayed sales, but December recovered to a record $74.9 million in fourth-quarter apparel revenue; rain jackets and children’s jackets also performed well, and high jacket margins lifted profit disproportionately.
children.text: Apparel revenue grew 10.7 percent to 237.0 million dollars, and jackets made up just under half of it. The Ridgeline insulated jacket was again our best-selling product, with 182,000 sold. We moved all insulated jackets to recycled polyester fill and certified down, at no extra cost to customers. The warm November in Europe delayed jacket sales, but most of them came back in December, so fourth-quarter apparel revenue still reached a record 74.9 million dollars. Rain jackets also had a good year after the wet spring in the United Kingdom, and sales of children's jackets doubled after we added sizes for children from four years old. Jackets carry our highest margins, so their strong fourth quarter lifted profit more than revenue.

children.title: Base layers and everyday wear
children.summary: The new merino base-layer range generated $9 million in its first year, mainly through the company website, while everyday wear grew 6 percent. Apparel returns fell to 8.1 percent after the website added fit guides, body-shape photos, and customer size ratings. The section also explains merino’s benefits for multi-day hikes, notes that all wool is sourced from Responsible Wool Standard-certified farms in Australia and New Zealand, and describes plans for women’s cuts of every base layer in 2027.
children.text: The new merino base-layer range added 9 million dollars in its first year, mostly through our own website, where customers who bought one piece often came back for a second. Everyday wear, such as fleeces and walking trousers sold for city use, grew 6 percent. Returns of apparel fell to 8.1 percent of sales after we added fit guides, body-shape photos and customer size ratings to the website. For 2027 we plan a women's cut of every base layer. Merino is a natural wool that keeps its warmth when wet and does not hold smells, which makes it popular for multi-day hikes. All the merino comes from farms certified to the Responsible Wool Standard in Australia and New Zealand.

children.title: Footwear
children.summary: Footwear revenue rose 7.2% to $143.5 million, driven entirely by hiking boots; trail-running shoe revenue was flat at $41 million and its share of footwear revenue declined. The sections describe boot sales, fitting and repair services, and upcoming product plans, alongside trail-shoe assortment changes, customer ratings, and a redesigned range planned for March 2027.

children.title: Hiking boots
children.summary: Footwear revenue rose 7.2% to $143.5 million, entirely from hiking boots, which grew 13%; the recycled-rubber-sole Summit mid-height boot became the best-selling shoe. Boots sell especially well in company stores, supported by fitting services and new store openings, while online customers can exchange sizes for free. In 2027, the company will begin offering worn-sole replacement in ten stores in the United States and Germany, starting with boots because they are the footwear product most often returned for repair.
children.text: Footwear revenue grew 7.2 percent to 143.5 million dollars, all of it from hiking boots, which grew 13 percent. The Summit mid-height boot, made with a recycled rubber sole, became our best-selling shoe. Boots sell best in our own stores, where customers can try them on and have them fitted, so new stores helped. In 2027 we will launch a footwear repair service that replaces worn soles, starting in ten stores in the United States and Germany. Every boot now comes with a free fitting in store, and online customers can exchange a size for free. Boots are also the footwear product customers most often bring back for repair, which is why the new repair service starts with them.

children.title: Trail-running shoes
children.summary: Trail-running shoe revenue was flat at $41 million, while the category’s share of footwear revenue fell from 31% to 29%. The company resisted unprofitable price cuts, reduced its range from 14 models to 9, and moved discontinued models to outlet stores; customer ratings remained strong at 4.6 out of 5. A redesigned, lighter range with a wider toe box is scheduled to go on sale in March 2027.
children.text: Trail-running shoe revenue was flat at 41 million dollars. Several large brands cut prices sharply during the year, and we chose not to follow them below the point where we would lose money. We reduced the number of trail-running models from 14 to 9 to focus on the best sellers, and sold the rest through our outlet stores. A redesigned range, lighter and with a wider toe box that customers asked for, goes on sale in March 2027. Trail-running shoes made up 29 percent of footwear revenue, down from 31 percent. Despite the price competition, customer ratings for our trail-running shoes stayed among the highest in the market, at 4.6 out of 5.

children.title: Equipment
children.summary: This section covers equipment revenue and product performance across tents, packs, sleeping bags, and accessories. Tents drove growth, with revenue up 21% to $61 million, led by the Aspen ultralight range; packs, sleeping bags, and accessories generated $52 million, up 9%. It can answer questions about best-selling products, product improvements, returns, suppliers, and seasonal or related-product sales.

children.title: Tents
children.summary: Tents drove equipment growth: revenue rose 21% to $61 million, led by the Aspen ultralight range, which sold 41,000 units and sold out twice after its April launch. The company added a second supplier in Vietnam to meet demand; two-person tents were the best-selling size, and tent returns were just 2.3% of sales, the lowest rate among product groups.
children.text: Equipment revenue grew 15.0 percent to 113.0 million dollars, the fastest of our three segments. Tents led the way: the Aspen ultralight range, launched in April, sold 41,000 units and sold out twice in the summer. We added a second supplier in Vietnam to meet demand. Fourth-quarter equipment sales were lower than the third quarter, as is usual after the camping season, which is why the segment's quarterly revenue peaks in the third quarter. Tents made up 61 million dollars of equipment revenue, up 21 percent, and we sold more two-person tents than any other size. Tent returns were just 2.3 percent of sales, the lowest of any product group.

children.title: Packs and accessories
children.summary: Packs, sleeping bags, and accessories generated $52 million in equipment revenue, up 9 percent. The Trailhead 45L pack won two industry awards; the company replaced its high-return, cheapest sleeping bags with a mid-priced range using recycled insulation, and designed new packs with replaceable buckles and straps. Accessories benefited from the Aspen tent launch, are often purchased with tents, and sell strongly as gifts in December.
children.text: Backpacks, sleeping bags and smaller accessories such as stoves and headlamps made up 52 million dollars of equipment revenue, up 9 percent. The Trailhead 45 litre pack won two industry awards. We stopped selling our cheapest sleeping bags, which had the highest return rates, and replaced them with a mid-priced range filled with recycled insulation. Accessories are often bought alongside a tent, so they also benefited from the Aspen launch. Packs are the equipment product most often brought to our repair counters, so every new pack has replaceable buckles and straps. Accessories also make good gifts, and they sell strongly in December.

children.title: Operations
children.summary: Covers the company’s store network and performance, distribution and delivery operations, and workforce, benefits, and development. It includes 2026 store changes and 2027 opening plans, logistics improvements and delivery timelines, and employee representation, turnover, survey results, and training. Answers questions about store counts and services, shipping and returns, and the company’s people and workplace programs.

children.title: Stores
children.summary: Covers the store network and its 2026 changes: seven openings, one closure, 64 stores at year end, and plans for six more openings in 2027. It describes smaller store formats, 5% sales-per-square-metre growth at stores open over a year, and how free online-order collection and in-store events brought customers and participants into stores. Answers questions about store locations and counts, store performance, future openings, and customer services and events.
children.text: We opened seven stores in 2026, three in the United States, two in Japan, one in the United Kingdom and one in Canada, and closed one in a shopping mall where footfall had fallen. That leaves 64 stores at year end. New stores are smaller than our older ones, about 400 square metres, with a repair counter and a space for local hiking clubs to meet. Sales per square metre in stores open for more than a year grew 5 percent. Six more stores will open in 2027. Every store also offers free collection of online orders, which brought 380,000 customers into our stores in 2026. Store staff run free guided walks and introductory camping evenings, which drew 26,000 people in 2026.

children.title: Distribution and logistics
children.summary: North American online orders and store deliveries ship from Columbus, Ohio, while European orders use a partner warehouse near Rotterdam; the company serves 31 countries and offers next-day delivery in major U.S. and Canadian cities. Ohio’s 2026 sorting machines reduced per-order handling costs by 14%, and returns are processed within three days of reaching a warehouse. European delivery averages four days and is expected to fall to two days when the company’s Netherlands distribution centre opens in 2028; construction is scheduled to start in 2027.
children.text: All online orders and store deliveries in North America leave from our distribution centre in Columbus, Ohio, and European orders from a partner warehouse near Rotterdam. In 2026 we installed automatic sorting machines in Ohio, which cut the cost of handling each order by 14 percent. Orders in Europe take four days on average to arrive. A second distribution centre of our own, in the Netherlands, will start construction in 2027 and open in 2028, bringing that down to two days. We ship to customers in 31 countries, and next-day delivery is available in the largest cities of the United States and Canada. Returns are processed within three days of reaching the warehouse.

children.title: Our people
children.summary: Covers workforce growth, gender representation, employee turnover and survey results. It also reports employee benefits and development, including a gear allowance, higher U.S. store minimum wages, and product-specialist training for 120 store employees.
children.text: We ended the year with 2,140 employees, up from 1,960, most of the new jobs in stores and in equipment design. 47 percent of our employees and 42 percent of managers are women. Voluntary staff turnover fell to 14 percent from 17 percent, and 81 percent of employees took part in our annual survey, with 76 percent saying they would recommend Fernhill as a place to work. Every employee received a 500 dollar gear allowance, and we raised the minimum hourly wage in our stores to 19 dollars in the United States. We also trained 120 store employees as product specialists through our internal programme.

children.title: Sustainability
children.summary: Covers the company’s sustainability performance and practices across materials, emissions, and suppliers. Materials account for 58% of fabric purchases, with a 75% target by 2028; emissions declined in 2026, and the section includes a table comparing 2025 and 2026 figures and changes, alongside 2030 reduction targets. It also describes supplier factory audits, findings and remediation, wage checks, and the publication of supplier details.

children.title: Materials
children.summary: Recycled and responsibly sourced materials accounted for 58% of fabric purchased, up from 49%, with a goal of 75% by 2028; recycled fabrics cost 6% more on average, a cost absorbed in margins. All jacket down and wool meet the Responsible Down Standard and Responsible Wool Standard, respectively, and PFAS water repellents were eliminated from all products in July 2026. The section also covers recycled polyester from plastic bottles, trials of fabric recycled from old Fernhill jackets, and materials scores used in designers’ targets.
children.text: Recycled and responsibly sourced materials made up 58 percent of the fabric we bought, up from 49 percent. Our goal is 75 percent by 2028. All down used in our jackets is certified to the Responsible Down Standard, and all wool to the Responsible Wool Standard. We stopped using fluorinated water repellents, known as PFAS, in every product in July 2026, a year earlier than we had promised. Recycled fabrics cost on average 6 percent more, which we absorbed in our margins. Most of our recycled polyester is made from plastic bottles, and in 2026 we began testing fabric recycled from old Fernhill jackets. Our product designers now receive a materials score for every new product, which counts towards their own targets.

children.title: Emissions
children.summary: Emissions from own operations and purchased electricity fell 18% to 8,900 tonnes of CO₂e in 2026; 41 of 64 stores use renewable electricity. Scope 3 emissions from suppliers, shipping and products fell 6% to 212,000 tonnes, mainly due to shifting more goods from air to sea. The table compares 2025 and 2026 emissions and changes; targets for 2030, relative to 2022, are to halve scope 1 and 2 emissions and cut scope 3 emissions by 30%.
children.text:
Emissions from our own operations and the electricity we buy fell 18 percent, as 41 of our 64 stores now run on renewable electricity. Emissions from our suppliers' factories and from shipping, which make up most of our footprint, fell 6 percent, mainly because more goods travelled by sea instead of air. Our target is to halve emissions from our own operations and cut supplier and shipping emissions by 30 percent by 2030, compared with 2022. The table shows emissions in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent.

| Emissions (tonnes of CO2 equivalent) | 2026 | 2025 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Own operations and electricity (scopes 1 and 2) | 8,900 | 10,850 | -18% |
| Suppliers, shipping and products (scope 3) | 212,000 | 225,500 | -6% |

children.title: Suppliers and factory audits
children.summary: About 70% of products are made by 46 supplier factories in Vietnam, Bangladesh, and Portugal; all receive unannounced independent audits at least annually against standards covering wages, hours, safety, and union rights. In 2026, audits found 112 issues—mostly overtime and fire-exit concerns—with 97 fixed by year-end and plans in place for the rest; the company ended its relationship with a factory that blocked auditors. The company publishes supplier names and addresses, updated every six months, and checks wages against local living-wage estimates as well as legal minimums.
children.text: About 70 percent of our products are made by 46 supplier factories in Vietnam, Bangladesh and Portugal. Every factory is audited at least once a year by an independent firm, unannounced, against our supplier code, which covers wages, working hours, safety and the right to join a union. In 2026 the audits found 112 issues, mostly about overtime and fire exits; 97 were fixed by year end and the rest have dated plans. We stopped working with one factory that refused to let auditors in. We publish the names and addresses of all our supplier factories on our website, updated every six months. Wages at our suppliers are checked against local living-wage estimates, not only against the legal minimum.

children.title: Governance
children.summary: This section covers board composition, attendance, director roles and committee responsibilities, annual re-election, and fixed-fee compensation; a table lists directors, their roles, and joining years. It also explains the CEO’s 2026 pay and performance-based share awards, bonus metrics, CEO-to-median-employee pay ratio, executive share-holding requirements, and annual benchmarking against ten comparable companies.

children.title: Board of directors
children.summary: The board has seven directors, including four independent directors and three women; all attended at least eight of its nine meetings in 2026. The table lists each director’s role and joining year, including committee chairs. The section also explains committee responsibilities, annual re-election, and fixed-fee compensation without bonuses or shares.
children.text:
The board has seven directors: the chair, the chief executive, the chief financial officer and four independent directors. Three of the seven are women. The board met nine times in 2026, and every director attended at least eight meetings. Its audit committee oversees financial reporting and risk, and its people committee sets executive pay. All directors stand for re-election at the annual meeting each May. Directors are paid a fixed fee and receive no bonus or shares, so that they can judge the executives' performance independently.

children.title: Executive pay
children.summary: Reports the chief executive’s 2026 total pay of $2.6 million, broken down into salary, annual bonus, and shares that vest in 2029 if targets are met. Explains the bonus metrics, the CEO-to-median-employee pay ratio and its change from 2025, executive share-holding requirements, and annual benchmarking against ten comparable outdoor and sports companies.
children.text: The chief executive's total pay for 2026 was 2.6 million dollars: a salary of 850,000 dollars, an annual bonus of 940,000 dollars and shares worth about 810,000 dollars that vest in 2029 if targets are met. Half of the annual bonus depends on operating income, a quarter on direct sales and a quarter on sustainability targets, including recycled materials and emissions. The chief executive's pay was 48 times the median pay of our employees, down from 52 times in 2025. Shares granted to executives must be held for at least two years after they vest. The people committee compares executive pay with ten similar companies in the outdoor and sports market every year.

children.title: Risks
children.summary: Covers the company’s key operational and financial risks: supply-chain disruptions and cost volatility, weather-driven seasonality, foreign-exchange movements, and cybersecurity or customer-data incidents. It explains mitigation measures—including supplier diversification and inventory buffers, staged buying and forecasting, currency hedges, and security controls—and notes remaining exposures such as fourth-quarter revenue concentration, margin pressure from discounting, and unhedged yen risk. There are no tables or images.

children.title: Supply chain
children.summary: About 70% of products are made by suppliers in Vietnam, Bangladesh, and Portugal, leaving deliveries vulnerable to disruptions such as natural disasters, political unrest, or pandemics. The company dual-sources its top 50 products across countries and keeps eight weeks of best-seller stock; these measures prevented stockouts during a nine-day Vietnam port closure in 2026. The section also covers risks to gross margin from volatile shipping prices and rising trade tariffs.
children.text: About 70 percent of our products are made by suppliers in Vietnam, Bangladesh and Portugal. A disruption at a major supplier or port, from a natural disaster, political unrest or a pandemic, could delay deliveries for months. We now buy every one of our top 50 products from at least two suppliers in different countries, and we keep eight weeks of stock of our best sellers. Shipping prices can also change quickly, which affects our gross margin. In 2026 a typhoon closed a port in Vietnam for nine days; because of these measures, no store ran out of a top-selling product. Rising trade tariffs between countries could also raise the cost of the products we import.

children.title: Weather and seasonality
children.summary: This section explains how a warm winter can reduce jacket sales and a wet summer can weaken camping-equipment demand, putting a significant share of annual revenue at risk—especially because nearly a third is earned in the fourth quarter. It covers mitigation through year-round products, staged winter-stock orders, and long-range weather forecasts, and notes that discounting jackets in a mild winter can reduce gross margin by about one percentage point.
children.text: A warm winter lowers demand for jackets, our most profitable products, and a wet summer lowers demand for camping equipment. Almost a third of annual revenue is earned in the fourth quarter, so a poor season can affect the whole year's results, as the warm November in Europe showed in 2026. To reduce this risk we are growing products sold all year round, such as base layers and everyday wear, and we order winter stock in two rounds, so we can cut the second order if demand is weak. We also track long-range weather forecasts when deciding how much winter stock to order. In a mild winter, discounts on jackets can take about one point off our gross margin.

children.title: Currency
children.summary: Most costs are in US dollars, while 38% of revenue comes from euros and pounds, creating risk that a stronger dollar reduces reported revenue and profit. The company hedges about 70% of expected currency needs over the next 12 months with forward contracts, used only to protect expected cash flows; in 2026, currency movements reduced reported revenue by about $3.1 million but had almost no effect on operating income. Japanese stores create a small, currently unhedged yen exposure.
children.text: Most costs are in US dollars, while 38 percent of revenue is earned in euros and pounds. If the dollar strengthens, that revenue is worth fewer dollars, and our profit falls. We hedge about 70 percent of expected currency needs for the next twelve months using forward contracts, which fix the exchange rate in advance. In 2026, currency movements reduced reported revenue by about 3.1 million dollars and had almost no effect on operating income because of these hedges. We do not use currency contracts to speculate, only to protect expected cash flows. Our stores in Japan add a small exposure to the yen, which is not yet hedged.

children.title: Cyber security and data
children.summary: More than 40% of revenue comes through the website and app, which hold personal details for about 4 million customers; an outage or data exposure could harm sales and trust. The company does not store card numbers, encrypts passwords, offers optional two-step sign-in, conducts external security tests twice a year, and trains employees. It reported no serious security incident in 2026; the audit committee reviews security plans twice yearly, and the company carries cyber-attack insurance.
children.text: More than 40 percent of our revenue now comes through our website and app, which hold the personal details of about 4 million customers. An attack that took the website offline in a busy season or exposed customer data would cost us sales and trust. We do not store card numbers ourselves, we test our systems with outside security firms twice a year, and every employee takes security training. We had no serious security incident in 2026. The audit committee reviews our security plans twice a year, and we hold insurance against the cost of a cyber attack. Customer passwords are stored in encrypted form, and customers can turn on two-step sign-in in the app.

children.title: Outlook for 2027
children.summary: The company expects 2027 revenue of $530–550 million and an operating margin of about 12%, with six new stores, a Netherlands distribution centre, and a footwear repair service planned. Capital spending is expected to reach about $30 million; equipment is forecast to grow fastest, while redesigned trail-running shoes are expected to return footwear to growth in the second half. The outlook assumes normal weather and no major supplier disruption, and first-half results are due at the end of July.
children.text: We expect revenue of 530 to 550 million dollars and an operating margin of about 12 percent. We plan to open six new stores, start building a second distribution centre in the Netherlands, and launch a footwear repair service. Capital spending is expected to be about 30 million dollars, higher than in 2026 because of the distribution centre. We expect equipment to keep growing fastest, helped by a new range of ultralight sleeping bags, and the redesigned trail-running shoes to return that range to growth in the second half of the year. These figures assume normal weather and no major disruption to our suppliers, as described under Risks. We will report our results for the first half of 2027 at the end of July.
